title: Collaborative Pi Durable

talking_points.point: This fork lets Alice and Bob instruct the same coding agents in one project folder.
details: Example: Alice starts a change; Bob sees it, adds a follow-up and asks another agent to review the files.

talking_points.point: The engineering work is shared control, saved requests and explicit failure handling.
details: Technical: a harness [software running the model/tool loop] already existed in Durable. We extended it rather than rebuilding that loop.

demo: Keep two browser profiles ready as Alice and Bob. Do not display their access tokens.
fallback: Use the recorded local screenshot if the website is unavailable.
limit: This is a trusted-team prototype; ordinary coding writes are not generally conflict-safe.
transition: First, what changes when a second person joins the same agents?

title: Two people share the same agent history

talking_points.point: Bob sees Alice's work in the same agent conversation; he does not need to copy it into another chat.
details: Example: Alice asks OpenAI to add search. Bob adds: "Handle empty searches too." Both instructions keep their author names.

talking_points.point: A second person can affect another person's work, so queueing and shared control matter.
details: Example: Bob's follow-up waits if OpenAI is busy. Stop affects that shared agent and its queued inputs, including Alice's.
Technical: a lane [one named agent's conversation and queue] is shared by both users; it is not a private copy per browser.

talking_points.point: A second agent can inspect the same files while keeping its own conversation history.
details: Example: Bob asks Ollama to review the search implementation. This is a user-directed request, not automatic delegation between agents.

demo: Point to Alice and Bob in two browser profiles.
Point to OpenAI and Ollama, matching the actual two-user/two-agent default.
fallback: Walk through the three rows on the slide; an access matrix is unnecessary.
limit: We show attribution and ordering, not automatic agreement between conflicting human requirements.
transition: Here is the same handoff in the web app.

title: Demo: one person hands work to another

talking_points.point: Show Bob observing and continuing Alice's request on the same agent.
details: Example: Alice creates handoff.txt; Bob updates that same file through the shared OpenAI conversation.

talking_points.point: Check the real file, not just the model's answer.
details: Example: after Bob's edit, both pages refresh Workspace files and see the updated text.

talking_points.point: The second agent is another participant in the same workspace.
details: Example: Bob asks Ollama to read the file. Its separate history does not require a separate copy of the project.

demo: Alice to OpenAI: "Create handoff.txt containing exactly DRAFT. Then reply DONE."
Bob observes Alice's instruction, then tells the same agent: "Replace DRAFT with REVIEWED in handoff.txt. Then reply DONE."
Both refresh Workspace files. If rehearsed latency permits, Bob asks Ollama to read handoff.txt; otherwise show the recorded result.
fallback: Use the historical local Ollama screenshot and describe the handoff as a planned live sequence.
limit: The screenshot is local recorded evidence. Fast completion may hide queueing; GCP Ollama latency is still being investigated.
transition: Now trace which part of Pi accepts, saves and runs that shared request.

title: Where the collaboration rules live

talking_points.point: The web host identifies the user; the Durable package owns the collaboration rules.
details: Example: the host maps a token to Alice, then the package checks that Alice belongs to the project.
Technical: authentication [who is calling] and authorization [what that person may do] are separate checks.

talking_points.point: We reused Durable's execution and storage rather than adding a second queue in the web server.
details: Example: the saved request and work enter Durable together, avoiding a handoff gap between two queues.

talking_points.point: Coding-agent is a separate Pi application; our demo runs Durable directly.
details: Technical: coding-agent has its own CLI/SDK [terminal application/programming interface]. Durable already had a separate model/tool loop before our fork.
Technical: Chord supplies selected state/watch utilities here; Pi AI handles model-provider communication.

demo: Trace Alice → web host → Durable collaboration → model/tools → shared files.
fallback: Use the responsibility table; no source-code tour is needed.
limit: One owning runtime controls each store/workspace. This does not provide multi-machine availability.
transition: Saving the request is separate from waiting for its model answer.

title: Saving a request is separate from its answer

talking_points.point: Accepted means the instruction was saved, not that the model finished it.
details: Example: Alice sees "Accepted durably" while her instruction remains queued.
Technical: a receipt [saved acceptance record] and executable work are committed in one transaction [database changes saved together].

talking_points.point: Retrying the original request ID finds its existing receipt; sending the same text again creates new work.
details: Example: Retry same command preserves the ID. Copy/paste followed by a new Send generates another ID.
Technical: identity includes project/thread, user, agent and request ID. A thread [shared project] groups the participants and workspace.

talking_points.point: A missing acknowledgement can leave the browser unsure whether acceptance happened.
details: Example: the save succeeds but the network reply is lost. Retry the original ID; do not invent a new ID to check status.
Technical: the live receipt is in <COLLAB_DATA>/thread.sqlite. Reload/relogin currently loses the browser's pending retry ID, not the server record.

demo: Point to an accepted request and its queued/running/completed status.
Explain Retry same command using the lost-reply example; there is no GUI button to force that network failure.
fallback: Read the ID example on the slide; do not deliberately break the presentation connection.
limit: One accepted command can still involve several model calls or file operations.
transition: The activity view shows those later stages separately.

title: Activity shows requests, tools and current files

talking_points.point: The activity feed shows who requested work and the status we observed.
details: Example: "Alice → OpenAI → running" establishes attribution and observed status, not task correctness.

talking_points.point: A tool result and a correct file change are different evidence.
details: Example: a write tool can complete successfully while producing the wrong implementation. Inspect the file and run relevant tests.

talking_points.point: The feed is recent evidence, not a complete audit history.
details: Technical: an audit log [retained sequence of all relevant events] is not implemented. The page retains 64 observations; tool records are agent-scoped when a particular user request cannot be identified reliably.

demo: Expand Activity, point to an author and a native tool summary, then inspect the file.
fallback: Use saved activity rather than waiting for a new model turn.
limit: Reconnect can miss intermediate transitions; tool summaries do not establish line-by-line file authorship.
transition: Even correctly completed requests can conflict when agents share files.

title: The stale-edit problem

talking_points.point: An edit is stale [based on outdated information] when another writer changes the file after the agent reads it.
details: Example: A and B read base. A writes base + alice; B later writes base + bob and removes Alice's change.

talking_points.point: Taking turns only during the final write does not make the earlier read current.
details: Technical: the existing per-file queue covers individual participating mutations, not the whole read → plan → write task.

talking_points.point: A dependency can change even when the destination file stays unchanged.
details: Example: B changes file2's API from a string parameter to an object. A's replacement of file1 can still use the old API; our current destination-only check does not detect this.

demo: Explain the three-step overwrite trace, then move directly to the managed conflict demonstration on slide 8.
fallback: Use the trace; racing two live models is unnecessary.
limit: Ordinary coding-agent tools, shell commands and Codex still permit these risks.
transition: The next slide demonstrates a narrow enforced check before publication.

title: Demo: generate, publish, resolve and reset

talking_points.point: Generate asks a selected model for replacement text; it does not write the file.
details: Example: both users retain Welcome/neutral. Alice proposes Hello/light; Bob proposes Hi from the team/dark.
Technical: each participant gets an isolated proposal-only conversation with no file/shell tools, even if both select the same model.

talking_points.point: Publish checks the saved original against the current file and refuses a stale proposal.
details: Example: Alice publishes first. Bob's old-base proposal is retained as a conflict while Alice's bytes stay unchanged.
Technical: this is optimistic concurrency control [prepare independently, validate before applying]. It checks one destination, not every dependency.

talking_points.point: The user resolves the conflict after generation has finished; the agent is not paused waiting for that decision.
details: Example: Bob explicitly chooses Hello/dark and publishes it. There is no automatic merge, re-draft, continuation or resolution notification to the model.
Technical: Reset creates a fresh round, refuses old-round actions and closes old generation. Up to 64 rounds are retained; an uncertain publication still requires inspection.

demo: Before the talk: reset and generate both proposals; disclose that generation was prepared in advance if model latency is high.
At this slide: show both original bases and generated proposals. Publish Alice, then Bob; inspect the retained conflict.
Bob explicitly enters "Greeting: Hello" and "Theme: dark", then publishes the reviewed resolution.
Reset for both users; show fresh defaults and unchanged normal coding histories. Preview uses fixed sample outputs, not prompt interpretation.
fallback: Run example 41 separately, or use the table as a labelled worked example. It needs no model key.
limit: Only the managed proposal path has this check. Ordinary coding writes remain unprotected.
transition: Enforcing a write check is separate from explaining peer changes to a model.

title: Agents know peers may change files

talking_points.point: We tell agents that their private history may not explain the current shared file.
details: Example: Ollama writes blue; GPT later changes it to green. Ollama should reread rather than assume its own previous edit failed.

talking_points.point: The added context contains a short policy and limited participant/request references, not everyone's conversations.
details: Technical: native [Durable-run] agents receive refreshed context before each model request. External agent applications receive it at turn open/resume.
Example: recent accepted work does not prove who changed a file or explain the user's resolution decision.

talking_points.point: This improves the information supplied to the model; it does not enforce correct behavior.
details: Example: another agent can change a dependency after a reread. Dependency-version checks and explicit resolution notices remain extensions.
Technical: input tokens [pieces of text processed by the model] increase, but no extra model call is required just to supply this context. Its latency/cost impact is unmeasured.

demo: Use the blue → green → reread example. Show a real peer-edit turn only after rehearsing its actual behavior.
fallback: Explain the example without waiting for another model call.
limit: There is no guaranteed model compliance, automatic file-author log or notification of every user resolution.
transition: We also need to distinguish saved requests from recoverable external effects.

title: What survives a crash

talking_points.point: Saved requests and results can survive a restart; an in-flight model call is not a saved running process.
details: Example: Alice's accepted instruction remains in SQLite [an embedded database file] when the app restarts.

talking_points.point: A file change can happen before its success is saved, making repetition unsafe.
details: Example: a tool appends hello; the host crashes before recording success. Repeating the operation could append hello twice.
Technical: database commits and workspace writes are separate operations. One accepted command is not a promise of one model call or one file effect.

talking_points.point: Uncertain external work is marked interrupted rather than automatically resent.
details: Technical: a dispatch marker [saved record that an external attempt may have been sent] is written before sending to Codex. A crash before send can therefore also abandon an attempt that never ran.
Example: Stop does not undo edits or prove every child process has exited.

demo: If rehearsed on disposable data, show saved history after an idle service stop/start. Keep active crash tests separate.
fallback: Explain append → crash → unknown outcome using the table.
limit: Native model calls may repeat under Durable recovery rules. Windows Bash shutdown and full Linux child cleanup remain unresolved checks.
transition: Codex has its own execution loop, which explains the special external boundary.

title: A model service versus an agent application

talking_points.point: A provider [service supplying model output] is different from a harness [software running conversation and tools].
details: Example: OpenAI and Ollama supply model output to Durable. Durable runs their tool loop.

talking_points.point: An external harness [separate agent application] runs its own model/tool loop outside Durable.
details: Example: Codex runs as another process. Our adapter [connector translating requests/events] sends work and tracks its result; it is not just another model URL.

talking_points.point: We reused T3's actual Codex client/protocol code, not its entire app.
details: Technical: protocol [request/event format] tests use scripted child processes and recorded messages. Real CLI [command-line application] initialization works, but a real authenticated coding turn/continuation is still unverified.

demo: Point to the OpenAI/Ollama names, then explain Codex as a separate optional execution path.
fallback: Use the two execution paths; no live Codex demonstration is required without verified authentication.
limit: Two native model providers do not prove two working agent applications. Other provider keys and real Codex authentication have separate checks.
transition: Here is the evidence we have for each claim.

title: What our checks establish

talking_points.point: Controlled tests force known timing; real-model checks establish actual integration.
details: Example: a test holds both reads before releasing either write. A separate real Ollama check verifies actual generated text, file bytes and reset.

talking_points.point: The load test exercised real HTTP and SQLite with simulated agent work.
details: Example: 1,200 commands completed in about ten minutes. A burst completed 81 and rejected 519 at the configured queue limit.
Technical: a soak [sustained workload] is not a real-model throughput benchmark. One observed start per accepted command is not a universal exactly-once guarantee.

talking_points.point: Every result needs its boundary stated.
details: Technical: 48 demo tests and 68 focused Durable tests passed in recorded runs; this is not the entire repository suite.
Example: local Ollama success does not prove GCP speed, real Codex behavior or correct handling of every crash.

demo: Show the saved load report or the portable Ollama proposal result. Do not run load on the presentation's live store.
fallback: Use the slide's counts and explain which work was simulated.
limit: Maximum throughput, token overhead and cloud performance remain unmeasured; GCP slow-chat diagnosis is still open.
transition: Deployment adds another set of operational checks.

title: GCP deployment and remaining checks

talking_points.point: The app runs on one VM [virtual machine] with saved data and a shared project folder.
details: Example: the sslip.io address routes to Caddy [server forwarding browser traffic securely to the app], which forwards to 127.0.0.1:4310.

talking_points.point: The cloud website is accessible, but model speed and recovery still need separate checks.
details: Example: regular Ollama chat on GCP can exceed 60 seconds while idle curl generation is fast. The cause has not been confirmed.
Technical: compare full model-request timing with browser delivery before attributing the delay to CPU, history or the proxy.

talking_points.point: A safe update rebuilds assets and restarts the single owner while preserving data and credentials.
details: Example: stop after agents are idle, back up, fetch the reviewed revision, build, start, then reload both pages.
Technical: a failure domain [things that fail together] includes the owning process, disk and VM/zone. Starting two owners on the same files is unsafe.

demo: Use only the actual tested URL/revision. Confirm service/model readiness before the interview; keep a local fallback ready.
fallback: Show the deployment path and explain the outstanding latency/restore checks.
limit: Do not generalize website access into proven recovery or performance. Confirm the latest revision, backup restoration, Linux child cleanup and hosted demonstration timing.
transition: Finish with what we delivered and the next protection to add.

title: What is implemented and what comes next

talking_points.point: Implemented: shared agents, saved request identity, visible activity, peer awareness and the controlled managed-file flow.
details: Example: two users can continue the same agent conversation and demonstrate a refused stale proposal with explicit resolution/reset.

talking_points.point: Next, make ordinary coding edits participate in a managed protocol and track the files their plans depend on.
details: Example: if file2's API changes, refuse A's file1 proposal and request a new plan before publishing.
Technical: read set [files the plan relied on] validation needs coordination through publication. Prompt reminders alone cannot provide it.

talking_points.point: Keep further extensions separate from the current take-home scope.
details: Example: automatic re-drafting after resolution, worktrees [separate checked-out directories], shared approvals and multiple owners need additional design/tests.
Technical: current priorities include GCP latency/rehearsal, real Codex coding/continuation and Linux cleanup/backup restoration.

demo: Return to the shared-agent or managed conflict view for questions. Use backup slides only when relevant.
fallback: End with the concrete delivered behaviors and the dependency-change example.
limit: Native rehearsal uses existing OpenAI/Ollama access; Codex needs separate authentication. Updated cloud code and acceptance checks are still required.
transition: Invite questions about file protection, recovery or the reused components.

title: Backup: file protection and dependencies

talking_points.point: Today's managed check validates the destination file, not every file used to plan an edit.
details: Example: file1 is unchanged, but file2 now requires an object instead of a string. The destination check can pass while the code is wrong.

talking_points.point: Dependency-aware checks record versions of the files read and validate them before publication.
details: Technical: a read set [files the plan relied on] must remain unchanged through validation/publication, or another writer can race the check. All relevant writers must participate.

talking_points.point: Whole-task ownership or separate worktrees offer different trade-offs.
details: Example: ownership makes peers wait; worktrees allow isolated edits but require reviewed integration and tests.
Technical: a lease [permission that expires] cannot stop an old shell. T3's inspected startup lease ends before its provider turn, so it is not a whole-task lock.

demo: Use the file1/file2 example to compare destination checks, dependency checks, ownership and worktrees.
fallback: Walk through the rows without opening another tool.
limit: Dependency validation, whole-task ownership, automatic merging and unrestricted shell protection are not implemented.
transition: Return to the relevant main slide after answering.

title: Backup: trusted users and shared control

talking_points.point: The host identifies users, and the package checks their membership.
details: Example: a message saying "I am Alice" does not authenticate its sender. A valid token maps to Alice before the package receives the command.

talking_points.point: Every current member can see all agent conversations and stop shared work.
details: Example: Bob's Stop also affects Alice's queued requests on that agent. There are no private per-user agent histories or dynamic roles.

talking_points.point: A workspace directory is not a sandbox [enforced restriction on what a process can access].
details: Example: ordinary coding-agent shell tools can access files available to the service account outside that directory.
Technical: queue limits bound admitted work, not money spent, hostile execution or fairness between users.

demo: Explain the trusted-team boundary; do not demonstrate secret access or destructive commands.
limit: Public URL access still requires application authentication; hostile multi-tenant execution is outside this prototype.
transition: Return to the shared-control or deployment discussion.

title: Backup: reconnect and request retries

talking_points.point: Reconnect fetches the latest view; it does not replay every missed token or status change.
details: Technical: SSE [server-to-browser updates over HTTP] carries snapshots [recent views]. Saved message history can be loaded separately.

talking_points.point: A slow viewer keeps a recent pending view rather than every intermediate update.
details: Example: Bob may jump from running to completed after reconnect, without seeing each tool step.
Technical: coalescing [replacing an older pending view with the newest] limits that buffer, not all operating-system or process memory.

talking_points.point: The server's saved receipt and the browser's pending retry ID have different lifetimes.
details: Example: Retry same command reuses the ID; reload/relogin can lose it. Copy/paste with a new Send creates another command, even with identical text.
Technical: a lost acceptance reply does not prove rejection. Storage errors can occur after commit; stop the failed owner before reopening and retry the original identity.

demo: Reload only an idle/acknowledged browser view, sign in and show restored history without submitting another instruction.
fallback: Use the same-ID retry versus new-ID Send example.
limit: There is no complete event journal or persisted browser retry ledger. Discarding a retry does not cancel accepted work.

title: Backup: design choices and AI assistance

talking_points.point: I directed the project toward extending Durable and demonstrating shared behavior with explicit limits.
details: Example: evolving the fork, requiring actual T3 reuse and challenging the original access-matrix demo were deliberate scope decisions.

talking_points.point: Existing Pi components and T3 code remain credited; AI assisted implementation and documentation.
details: Example: I should be able to explain the receipt transaction and stale-edit trace without relying on an assistant's wording.

talking_points.point: The original twenty-hour target shaped scope; it is not a measured elapsed-time claim.
details: Technical: one owner, fixed membership and one managed file reduce delivery complexity. Broader protection requires additional work and evidence.

demo: Answer with one design choice, one concrete trace and one test boundary.
fallback: Use the file conflict or lost-reply example.
limit: Phrase personal ownership truthfully; do not imply all upstream code or validation was written manually.
